lessons.title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
lessons.enquiry: Out of the ashes: How did the devastating legacy of the First World War forge the Weimar Republic, and were the democratic foundations of its new Constitution fatally flawed from the start?

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry examines the chaotic birth of the Weimar Republic from the ashes of military defeat in late 1918, exploring the impact of the First World War and naval blockade, the Kiel Mutiny and revolution, the abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II, the creation of the provisional government under Friedrich Ebert, and the democratic architecture and fatal structural flaws of the 1919 Weimar Constitution.

objectives.objective: Explain how military collapse and civilian starvation forced German leaders to seek an immediate armistice in 1918.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2]. Highlight that Germany’s debt had tripled, 2 million soldiers were dead, and 750,000 civilians died of malnutrition and hypothermia under the British naval blockade, forcing General Ludendorff to demand a truce.
objectives.question: How did the British naval blockade and civilian starvation contribute to the political collapse of Imperial Germany in autumn 1918?

objectives.objective: Analyse why the Kiel Mutiny sparked a nationwide revolution that forced Kaiser Wilhelm II to abdicate.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2]. Explain that sailors refused a suicidal final attack, forming workers’ and soldiers’ councils that swept across Germany until Prince Max of Baden announced the Kaiser’s abdication on 9 November 1918.
objectives.question: Why did the naval mutiny at Kiel spread so rapidly into a popular revolution across German cities?

objectives.objective: Assess how Friedrich Ebert established the provisional government and secured the army’s loyalty via the Ebert-Groener Pact.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [3.1]–[3.2] and Source A (Armed revolutionaries in Berlin). Emphasize that Ebert signed the Armistice on 11 November and allied secretly with General Groener to protect the government against communist revolution.
objectives.question: Why did Friedrich Ebert make a secret alliance with the imperial military leadership to defend the new republic?

objectives.objective: Examine why the National Assembly met in Weimar to draft the new democratic constitution in early 1919.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [4.1]–[4.2]. Focus on the January 1919 elections, the 76% majority for pro-republican parties, and the relocation to the peaceful town of Weimar away from violent Berlin street riots.
objectives.question: Why was the National Assembly held in the provincial town of Weimar rather than the capital city of Berlin?

objectives.objective: Evaluate the structural strengths and fatal vulnerabilities of the 1919 Weimar Constitution, focusing on Proportional Representation and Article 48.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [5.1]–[5.2]. Contrast progressive democratic rights and female suffrage with the instability of coalition governments under PR and the dictatorial loophole of Article 48 presidential decrees.
objectives.question: Why did Proportional Representation and Article 48 emergency decrees prove to be fatal structural weaknesses in the Weimar Constitution?

source_context.Source A: On 9 November 1918, SPD leader Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed the German Republic from a window of the Reichstag to pre-empt Karl Liebknecht declaring a Soviet-style communist republic from the Berlin Palace. Hinge Question: Why did Scheidemann rush to proclaim a parliamentary republic from the Reichstag window without consulting party leader Friedrich Ebert?
source_context.Source B: Official press photograph taken in Berlin in November 1918 showing armed revolutionary soldiers and workers manning barricades. Hinge Question: How does Source A illustrate why Friedrich Ebert felt compelled to make a secret alliance with the imperial military officer corps in the Ebert-Groener Pact?
source_context.Source C: The official promulgated text of the Weimar Constitution passed by the National Assembly on 31 July 1919 and signed into law by President Friedrich Ebert on 11 August 1919. Hinge Question: Why did the inclusion of Article 48 in the Weimar Constitution ultimately prove more dangerous to democracy than the proportional representation voting system?
source_context.Source D: On the morning of 9 November 1918, Chancellor Prince Max von Baden unilaterally announced the Kaiser's abdication to prevent a general strike from escalating into a bloody revolution, handing the Chancellorship to SPD leader Friedrich Ebert. Hinge Question: Why did Prince Max von Baden announce the Kaiser's abdication before Wilhelm II had personally signed an official instrument of renunciation?
source_context.Source E: In February 1919, following democratic elections with an 83% turnout, Friedrich Ebert opened the National Assembly in Weimar, seeking to build democratic legitimacy while warning Allied victors at Versailles against crushing terms. Hinge Question: Why did Friedrich Ebert emphasise both lawful democratic order at home and resistance to Allied vengeance abroad in his opening address?

learning_objectives.overarching: To understand the origins, establishment, and constitutional structure of the Weimar Republic.
scaffolded: Demonstrate precise knowledge of the catastrophic social, economic, and political conditions in Germany at the end of WWI that triggered the Kaiser's abdication.
Analyse the sequence of events from the Kiel mutiny to the declaration of the Republic, explaining why Friedrich Ebert and the SPD acted to prevent a communist revolution.
Evaluate the democratic strengths and structural weaknesses of the Weimar Constitution, particularly the 'fatal flaws' of Proportional Representation and Article 48.

items.question: What was the Triple Entente in the First World War?
items.answer: An alliance between Britain, France, and Russia.

items.question: What was the Triple Alliance?
items.answer: An alliance between Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy.

items.question: What is a 'dictatorship'?
items.answer: A country ruled by a single leader with total power.

items.question: What is a 'democracy'?
items.answer: A system where the government is elected by the people.

items.question: What does 'abdicate' mean?
items.answer: When a monarch steps down from the throne.

items.question: What is a 'republic'?
items.answer: A country without a monarch, usually led by an elected president.

items.question: What does 'inflation' mean?
items.answer: The general increase in prices and fall in the purchasing value of money.

items.question: What is an 'armistice'?
items.answer: A formal agreement to stop fighting; a truce.

items.question: What does 'mutiny' mean?
items.answer: An open rebellion against the proper authorities, especially by soldiers or sailors.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Following the sudden signing of the [Armistice] in 1918, furious right-wing nationalists spread the [Dolchstoßlegende] (stab-in-the-back myth), branding the democratic politicians who surrendered as treasonous [November Criminals]. The new Weimar [Constitution] created a highly democratic system where the lower house, the [Reichstag], passed laws while the upper house, the [Reichsrat], could delay them. However, the voting system of [Proportional Representation (PR)] meant no single party could win a majority, leading to weak, constantly shifting [Coalition Government] alliances. This instability forced the President to frequently rely on the emergency powers granted by [Article 48] to rule by decree.

narrative_blocks.title: Mutiny on the High Seas: The Kiel Sailors' Revolt and Imperial Collapse (1918)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.1] By autumn 1918, Imperial Germany was facing imminent military collapse on the Western Front. Four grueling years of the British **Allied naval blockade** had strangled civilian supply lines, causing catastrophic food deprivation remembered as the **Turnip Winter starvation** that killed over 750,000 civilians. When naval commanders ordered a suicidal final sortie against the British fleet, exhausted sailors mutinied. [1.2] The rebellion exploded into the historic **Kiel naval mutiny** on 3 November 1918, where forty thousand armed sailors and dockworkers seized control of naval bases and raised socialist red banners. Within days, workers' and soldiers' councils took power across major cities, proving that imperial authorities had lost control of the armed forces and sparking the German Revolution.

sources.title: Source A: Armed Workers and Soldiers Manning Barricades in Berlin (November 1918)
sources.caption: Armed revolutionary fighters and deserting soldiers manning a street barricade constructed from giant newsprint rolls in the Berlin newspaper quarter during the revolutionary unrest of 1918–1919.
sources.desc: Archival press photograph of revolutionary fighters stationed behind heavy paper-roll barricades in Berlin, 1918–1919.
sources.provenance: Bundesarchiv Bild 183-B24522, Berlin Revolution, November 1918.
sources.hinge_question: How does Source A illustrate why Friedrich Ebert felt compelled to make a secret alliance with the imperial military officer corps in the Ebert-Groener Pact?
sources.source_context: Official press photograph taken in Berlin in November 1918 showing armed revolutionary soldiers and workers manning barricades. **Hinge Question:** How does Source A illustrate why Friedrich Ebert felt compelled to make a secret alliance with the imperial military officer corps in the Ebert-Groener Pact?
sources.context: Armed revolutionary soldiers and workers behind barricades in Berlin following the Kaiser's abdication.
sources.enquiry_question: How useful is Source A for an enquiry into the political instability confronting Friedrich Ebert's provisional government in 1918–1919?
sources.model_answer:
Content & Contextual Knowledge: Source A is exceptionally useful because it provides direct visual evidence of the total collapse of state policing and the armed paramilitary violence gripping the streets of Berlin. The photograph shows revolutionary fighters and deserting soldiers armed with military rifles barricaded behind giant industrial paper rolls in the Berlin newspaper quarter. This directly reflects historical reality: after the Kaiser’s abdication in November 1918, Ebert’s Council of People’s Representatives held nominal authority but possessed no loyal police force, leaving Berlin vulnerable to armed left-wing militias and revolutionary shop stewards who seized major government and newspaper buildings during the Spartacist Uprising in January 1919.

Provenance & Utility Evaluation: The provenance enhances its utility: as an authentic press photograph taken on the streets of Berlin during the revolutionary unrest (nature and origin), it captures the genuine street-level militarisation of German politics without artistic staging. However, its utility is focused specifically on the revolutionary epicenter of Berlin; it does not show the situation in rural southern Germany or regional cities where moderate local councils maintained civil order, nor does it illustrate the right-wing counter-violence of the Freikorps deployed by Ebert and Gustav Noske to crush the uprising.

paragraphs: [1.1] By autumn 1918, Imperial Germany was facing imminent military collapse on the Western Front. narrative_blocks.title: Flight to the Border: The Abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II and the Birth of the Republic (9 Nov 1918)
narrative_blocks.text: [2.1] On 9 November 1918, massive general strikes brought central Berlin to a standstill as revolutionary crowds surrounded government ministries. Isolated at military headquarters in Spa, the Emperor was warned by Field Marshal Hindenburg that the army would no longer obey his commands, compelling the formal **Kaiser Wilhelm abdication** and ending five centuries of proud Hohenzollern dynastic rule. [2.2] Wilhelm slipped into permanent **Dutch border exile** aboard a royal train the following morning. Meanwhile in Berlin, desperate to preempt communist revolutionaries from establishing a Soviet republic, Social Democratic leader **Philipp Scheidemann proclamation** announced the birth of the German Republic from a Reichstag window, handing provisional authority to SPD chancellor Friedrich Ebert to restore domestic order.

sources.title: Source B: Chancellor Prince Max von Baden's Proclamation of Kaiser Wilhelm II's Abdication (9 November 1918)
sources.caption: Imperial government decree issued by Prince Max von Baden announcing that Kaiser Wilhelm II and the Crown Prince had renounced the throne, transferring power to Friedrich Ebert.
sources.desc: Official printed government placard posted across Berlin on 9 November 1918 declaring the abdication of Wilhelm II.
sources.provenance: Imperial Chancellery, Berlin. Bundesarchiv R 43-I/1381, 9 November 1918.
sources.text: "The Kaiser and King has decided to renounce the throne. The Imperial Chancellor remains in office until the questions connected with the abdication of the Kaiser, the renouncing of the throne by the Crown Prince of the German Empire and of Prussia, and the setting up of a regency have been settled. He intends to propose to the Regent the appointment of Deputy Ebert to the Imperial Chancellorship and the drawing up of a bill for the immediate summoning of a German National Assembly."
sources.hinge_question: Why did Prince Max von Baden announce the Kaiser's abdication before Wilhelm II had personally signed an official instrument of renunciation?
sources.source_context: On the morning of 9 November 1918, Chancellor Prince Max von Baden unilaterally announced the Kaiser's abdication to prevent a general strike from escalating into a bloody revolution, handing the Chancellorship to SPD leader Friedrich Ebert. **Hinge Question:** Why did Prince Max von Baden announce the Kaiser's abdication before Wilhelm II had personally signed an official instrument of renunciation?
sources.context: Official decree issued by Prince Max von Baden announcing the abdication of the Kaiser on 9 November 1918.
sources.enquiry_question: Explain why Prince Max von Baden felt compelled to issue the proclamation in Source B on 9 November 1918.
sources.model_answer: Prince Max von Baden issued this proclamation as a desperate tactical gamble to prevent a full-scale communist revolution in Berlin. Following the Kiel naval mutiny in late October 1918, workers' and soldiers' councils had seized control of major cities across Germany, and on the morning of 9 November, a general strike paralysed the capital while garrison troops joined the protestors. Although Kaiser Wilhelm II had not yet formally signed a deed of abdication at military headquarters in Spa, Prince Max unilaterally announced the monarch’s renunciation to placate the revolutionary crowds, satisfy US President Woodrow Wilson’s demand for democratization as a condition for an armistice, and safely transfer the Chancellorship to moderate Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert before radical socialists could seize the state.

narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 2: Why did moderate Social Democrats rush to proclaim a republic before Communists did?
paragraphs: [2.1] On 9 November 1918, massive general strikes brought central Berlin to a standstill as revolutionary crowds surrounded government ministries. Isolated at military headquarters in Spa, the Emperor was warned by Field Marshal Hindenburg that the army would no longer obey his commands, compelling the formal **Kaiser Wilhelm abdication** and ending five centuries of proud Hohenzollern dynastic rule.

[2.2] Wilhelm slipped into permanent **Dutch border exile** aboard a royal train the following morning. Meanwhile in Berlin, desperate to preempt communist revolutionaries from establishing a Soviet republic, Social Democratic leader **Philipp Scheidemann proclamation** announced the birth of the German Republic from a Reichstag window, handing provisional authority to SPD chancellor Friedrich Ebert to restore domestic order.

narrative_blocks.title: The Armistice & The Ebert-Groener Pact: Forging a Secret Alliance with the Old Army (Nov 1918)
narrative_blocks.text: [3.1] Assuming power amid violent street fighting in Berlin, Social Democratic leader **Friedrich Ebert chancellor** sought desperately to stabilize the collapsing state. On 10 November 1918, Ebert concluded the telephone **Ebert-Groener army pact** with General Wilhelm Groener. The imperial officer corps promised to maintain domestic order and suppress communist insurrections, in exchange for Ebert guaranteeing military autonomy and defending the traditional officer caste against radical reform. [3.2] The following morning, the **Compiègne armistice signed** by civilian politician Matthias Erzberger in a railway carriage ended the First World War. While the armistice brought immediate peace, military commanders like Hindenburg and Ludendorff cynically avoided responsibility, shifting the stigma of surrender onto civilian republican politicians who were subsequently branded the "November Criminals" by right-wing nationalists across Germany.

sources.title: Source C: Proclamation of the Republic by Philipp Scheidemann (9 November 1918)
sources.text: Workers and soldiers! The German people have won all along the line! What is old and rotten has collapsed; militarism is finished! The Hohenzollerns have abdicated! Prince Max of Baden has handed over the office of Reich Chancellor to Ebert. Our friend Ebert will form a government of the people. Everything must be done for the people, everything by the people. Peace is assured. The new government will guarantee freedom and work. Long live the German Republic!

sources.caption: SPD leader Philipp Scheidemann proclaiming the German Republic from a window of the Reichstag building in Berlin to pre-empt a communist declaration.
sources.desc: Official press photograph of crowds gathered outside the Reichstag as Scheidemann proclaims the German Republic, 9 November 1918.
sources.provenance: Bundesarchiv Bild 146-1979-118-09, Berlin, 9 November 1918.

sources.context: SPD leader Philipp Scheidemann proclaims the German Republic from a window of the Reichstag on 9 November 1918.
sources.enquiry_question: Give two things you can infer from Source C about the establishment of the Weimar Republic in November 1918.
sources.model_answer:
• Inference 1: The republic was proclaimed amidst sudden, chaotic public excitement rather than an orderly constitutional ceremony.
    Detail from source: The photograph shows vast crowds of citizens packing the plaza outside the Reichstag to hear Scheidemann leaning out of an ordinary second-floor window.
  • Inference 2: Democratic leaders acted with extreme haste and urgency to take control of the state.
    Detail from source: Scheidemann is shown shouting the announcement informally from an open window without official preparation, state regalia, or prior consultation with SPD chairman Friedrich Ebert, in a desperate bid to pre-empt Karl Liebknecht declaring a communist soviet republic.

On 10 November 1918, Ebert concluded the telephone **Ebert-Groener army pact** with General Wilhelm Groener. The imperial officer corps promised to maintain domestic order and suppress communist insurrections, in exchange for Ebert guaranteeing military autonomy and defending the traditional officer caste against radical reform.

[3.2] The following morning, the **Compiègne armistice signed** by civilian politician Matthias Erzberger in a railway carriage ended the First World War. While the armistice brought immediate peace, military commanders like Hindenburg and Ludendorff cynically avoided responsibility, shifting the stigma of surrender onto civilian republican politicians who were subsequently branded the "November Criminals" by right-wing nationalists across Germany.

narrative_blocks.title: Flight from Berlin: The National Assembly Convened in Weimar (Jan–Feb 1919)
narrative_blocks.text: [4.1] In January 1919, nationwide democratic elections were held across Germany with an extraordinary eighty-three percent voter turnout. The moderate pro-republican parties secured a commanding parliamentary majority, establishing a stable **democratic coalition government** formed by the SPD, the Catholic Centre Party, and the German Democratic Party. Delegates subsequently elected moderate socialist leader **Friedrich Ebert president** of the newborn German Republic. [4.2] Because continuing street warfare and communist strikes made Berlin too dangerous for politicians, parliamentarians convened 150 miles south at the **Weimar National Assembly** in February 1919. Meeting inside the National Theatre, delegates drafted a new democratic constitution, deliberately associating the new state with the enlightened humanist traditions of Goethe and Schiller rather than authoritarian Prussian militarism.

sources.enquiry_question: How useful is Source D for an enquiry into the aims and political challenges facing the Weimar Republic's leadership in early 1919?
sources.model_answer:
Content & Contextual Knowledge: Source D is highly useful because it directly articulates the founding political ideology and external anxieties of the new republican leadership. Ebert declares that "arbitrary rule is ended forever" and that Germany's goal is "a republic rooted in social democracy and public justice", while sternly warning the Allies not to impose a "peace of vengeance that enslaves our working people." This aligns closely with historical knowledge: following the January 1919 elections where democratic parties won over 76% of the vote, Ebert convened the assembly in Weimar to draft a democratic constitution away from Berlin's street fighting. His speech reflects the intense pressure on the provisional government: they had to persuade the German people that democracy was legitimate, while desperately appealing to Allied negotiators in Paris not to impose devastating reparations that would cripple the new state.

Provenance & Utility Evaluation: The provenance provides exceptional insight into official republican strategy: as a keynote parliamentary address by the newly elected Reich President (nature and origin), it reveals how Ebert framed the transition from empire to democracy for both a domestic and international audience. However, the source presents an idealistic, public-facing defense of the regime; it omits the controversial, pragmatic compromises Ebert had secretly made to survive, specifically the Ebert-Groener Pact of 10 November 1918, in which the socialist government allied with the imperial military officer corps and deployed brutal Freikorps paramilitaries to execute left-wing revolutionaries like Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.

narrative_blocks.title: The Weimar Constitution: Progressive Universal Suffrage and Fatal Emergency Powers (Aug 1919)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.1] Promulgated on 11 August 1919, the Weimar Constitution established one of the most progressive democracies in the world. It guaranteed full freedom of speech, assembly, and religious worship, granting sweeping **universal suffrage rights** to all men and women aged twenty and above, creating an equitable voting framework that empowered ordinary citizens across Germany's eighteen federal states. [5.2] However, institutional flaws undermined its stability. The system of **proportional representation weakness** meant small fringe parties proliferated, making single-party majorities impossible and forcing endless unstable coalition governments. Most dangerously, **Article 48 emergency powers** empowered the president to suspend civil liberties and rule by presidential decree without parliamentary consent, providing a constitutional loophole that future dictators would exploit.

sources.enquiry_question: What does Source E suggest about the legal foundation and constitutional intentions of the new German Republic in 1919?
sources.model_answer: Source E demonstrates that the Weimar Republic sought to ground its sovereignty in formal constitutional legality, universal suffrage, and parliamentary democracy to replace the fallen Hohenzollern autocracy. Promulgated in the official Reichsgesetzblatt in August 1919, the constitution codified Europe's most progressive democratic framework, giving all men and women over twenty the vote and establishing an extensive bill of fundamental civil rights (Articles 109–118). However, it also enshrined institutional compromises that proved fatal: proportional representation encouraged unstable multi-party coalitions, while Article 48 granted the President sweeping emergency powers to bypass parliament and rule by decree, creating a constitutional mechanism that authoritarians would later exploit to dismantle democracy.

questions.question: Explain why the Weimar Republic was established in Germany in 1918–1919. [12 marks]
stimulus: Military defeat in the First World War
The Kiel Mutiny and German Revolution
bullet_points: Military defeat in the First World War
The Kiel Mutiny and German Revolution
questions.model:
One decisive reason for the Weimar Republic was military collapse and revolutionary unrest in late 1918. By October 1918, Germany faced inevitable defeat, prompting sailors at Kiel to mutiny rather than launch a suicidal assault against the British fleet. Mutiny spread across major cities, with workers' councils demanding the Kaiser’s abdication. Therefore, this established the Weimar Republic because mutiny and civil rebellion shattered the imperial regime's authority, forcing Kaiser Wilhelm II to abdicate on 9 November 1918 to prevent total state collapse.

Furthermore, the republic was created to preempt a violent Bolshevik-style communist takeover. With armed left-wing revolutionaries forming councils in Berlin, moderate SPD leader Friedrich Ebert moved quickly to proclaim a parliamentary democracy. Ebert secured the Ebert-Groener Pact with the army to crush radical extremism and preserve constitutional order. Therefore, this established the republic because moderate socialist politicians instituted a parliamentary democracy to satisfy popular demands for peace while preventing a violent Russian-style revolution.

Finally, a democratic republic was necessitated by Allied conditions for an immediate armistice. US President Woodrow Wilson stated the Allies would only negotiate peace with a democratic government representing the German people. Desperate to end the British naval blockade starving German cities, imperial commanders urged the transition to a civilian government. Therefore, this created the republic because creating a democratic constitution was the mandatory prerequisite for securing an armistice and halting catastrophic civilian starvation.

One reason was military defeat and the Kiel Mutiny in October 1918. German sailors refused to attack the British navy, and workers' councils formed across Germany. The generals told the Kaiser the war was lost, forcing him to abdicate on 9 November 1918.

Another reason was fear of communist revolution. Friedrich Ebert and the SPD declared a republic to prevent a Bolshevik-style takeover, and Allied leaders like Woodrow Wilson refused to negotiate peace with Germany unless it became a democracy.

questions.question: Question 3(a): Study Sources B and C. How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into the collapse of the Kaiserreich and the proclamation of the German Republic in November 1918? Explain your answer, using Sources B and C and your knowledge of the historical context. [8 marks]
questions.examiner_tip: Compare why BOTH announcements were rushed out on 9 November 1918: Prince Max acted from above to preserve constitutional order before Wilhelm II had formally signed his abdication, whereas Scheidemann spoke from the Reichstag window to stop radical Spartacists declaring a Soviet republic.
questions.model:
Source B is highly useful for investigating the collapse of the Kaiserreich because it captures how imperial authorities tried to manage revolution from above. Printed on the front page of the official Deutscher Reichsanzeiger on 9 November 1918, it announces that "The Kaiser and King has decided to renounce the throne" and proposes "the appointment of Deputy Ebert to the Imperial Chancellorship" alongside "the immediate summoning of a German National Assembly." Historically, following the Kiel Mutiny and general strikes in Berlin, Kaiser Wilhelm II at Spa still hesitated to abdicate. As an urgent official Chancellery proclamation issued unilaterally by Prince Max von Baden to calm rebellious crowds, its provenance is invaluable proof that moderate elites sacrificed the monarchy to prevent a violent Bolshevik-style upheaval.

Source C is equally useful because it reveals how popular street pressure forced moderate Social Democrats to proclaim a republic immediately. The press photograph shows SPD deputy Philipp Scheidemann leaning from a Reichstag window above hat-waving crowds, proclaiming "militarism is finished! The Hohenzollerns have abdicated!" and promising "freedom and work." In reality, Scheidemann improvised this speech without Ebert's permission after learning that Spartacist leader Karl Liebknecht was preparing to declare a Soviet republic from the Berlin Palace two hours later. Directed publicly at "Workers and soldiers!" massed outside parliament, its provenance exposes the intense competition for street legitimacy on 9 November 1918.

Taken together, Sources B and C complement each other effectively, contrasting the improvised constitutional handover inside the Chancellery with the urgent popular politics outside the Reichstag.

tier_2m.text: Source B is useful because it shows Prince Max von Baden announcing that Kaiser Wilhelm II was giving up the throne and handing power to Ebert. Source C is useful because it shows Philipp Scheidemann speaking from a Reichstag window to cheer the new German Republic.

tier_5m.title: 5/8 Partial Utility
tier_5m.text:
Source B is useful because the official notice declares that "The Kaiser and King has decided to renounce the throne" and proposes handing the Chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert. From my own knowledge, the Kiel naval mutiny and spreading workers' councils forced imperial ministers to act quickly before full revolution broke out.

Source C is also useful because the photograph shows Scheidemann addressing crowds outside the Reichstag, declaring "militarism is finished! The Hohenzollerns have abdicated!" However, while both sources show the monarchy collapsing on 9 November 1918, their contrasting political purposes require deeper evaluation.
tier_5m.verdict: AO3 Level 2 (5 marks). Developed judgement using specific details from Sources B and C supported by relevant contextual knowledge, though provenance evaluation remains brief or generic.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_8m.text:
Source B is highly useful for investigating the collapse of the Kaiserreich because it captures how imperial authorities tried to manage revolution from above. Printed on the front page of the official Deutscher Reichsanzeiger on 9 November 1918, it announces that "The Kaiser and King has decided to renounce the throne" and proposes "the appointment of Deputy Ebert to the Imperial Chancellorship" alongside "the immediate summoning of a German National Assembly." Historically, following the Kiel Mutiny and general strikes in Berlin, Kaiser Wilhelm II at Spa still hesitated to abdicate. As an urgent official Chancellery proclamation issued unilaterally by Prince Max von Baden to calm rebellious crowds, its provenance is invaluable proof that moderate elites sacrificed the monarchy to prevent a violent Bolshevik-style upheaval.

Source C is equally useful because it reveals how popular street pressure forced moderate Social Democrats to proclaim a republic immediately. The press photograph shows SPD deputy Philipp Scheidemann leaning from a Reichstag window above hat-waving crowds, proclaiming "militarism is finished! The Hohenzollerns have abdicated!" and promising "freedom and work." In reality, Scheidemann improvised this speech without Ebert's permission after learning that Spartacist leader Karl Liebknecht was preparing to declare a Soviet republic from the Berlin Palace two hours later. Directed publicly at "Workers and soldiers!" massed outside parliament, its provenance exposes the intense competition for street legitimacy on 9 November 1918.

Taken together, Sources B and C complement each other effectively, contrasting the improvised constitutional handover inside the Chancellery with the urgent popular politics outside the Reichstag.
tier_8m.verdict: AO3 Level 3 Top (8 marks). Balanced, sustained evaluation of both Sources B and C integrating precise source details, contextual own knowledge, and bespoke Nature/Origin/Purpose analysis tailored to the enquiry.

video.title: 1919-33: The Weimar Constitution | GCSE History Revision
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–05:00 | Lesson Phase: Starter Hook | Tone Alert: Analytical breakdown of the Weimar Constitution, Reichstag voting, and the emergency powers granted by Article 48.
video.viewing_task:
[01:30] Quick Check: What was the voting system used to elect deputies to the Weimar Reichstag, and how did it encourage coalitions?
[03:45] Disciplinary Question: Explain why Article 48 was described as a constitutional 'suicide pill' for the Republic.
video.model_answer: The Weimar Constitution used Proportional Representation, where the percentage of votes cast directly determined the percentage of seats won. Because it was almost impossible for a single party to win an outright majority, governments were forced into fragile, unstable coalitions. Article 48 allowed the President to rule by emergency decree without Reichstag consent, creating a legal route to dictatorship.

video.title: The Treaty of Versailles, What Did the Big Three Want? | Simple History
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–02:48 | Lesson Phase: Contextual Evidence | Tone Alert: Concise animated summary of the conflicting motivations of Clemenceau, Lloyd George, and Wilson in 1919.
video.viewing_task:
[00:50] Quick Check: Why did Georges Clemenceau demand the harshest possible terms against Germany at the Paris Peace Conference?
[02:10] Analysis: How did the final Treaty terms set up German resentment regarding the 'Diktat' and War Guilt clause?
video.model_answer: Clemenceau sought to permanently cripple Germany's military and economy to guarantee French security, given the devastation of northeastern France in WW1. The Germans felt betrayed because they were excluded from negotiations (a 'Diktat') and forced to sign Article 231 taking sole responsibility for causing the war.

video.title: Ten Minute History: The Weimar Republic and Nazi Germany | History Matters
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–04:00 | Lesson Phase: Synoptic Overview | Tone Alert: Rapid, dryly humorous animated overview tracking the German Revolution, abdication of the Kaiser, and the Dolchstoßlegende (stab-in-the-back myth).
video.viewing_task:
[01:10] Key Recall: Why did German military commanders like Ludendorff shift blame for the 1918 defeat onto civilian politicians in Berlin?
[02:40] Historical Inference: How did the 'November Criminals' myth undermine civilian trust in the new Weimar Republic from day one?
video.model_answer: Ludendorff and Hindenburg sought to protect the Prussian military elite's honour by falsely claiming the German army remained undefeated in the field and was 'stabbed in the back' by socialists and politicians at home. This propaganda branded the democratic founders as 'November Criminals', creating deep, enduring delegitimisation of the Republic.

tasks.text: Explain why the Weimar Republic was established in Germany in 1918–1919. [12 marks]
stimulus: Military defeat in the First World War
The Kiel Mutiny and German Revolution
tasks.model:
One major reason why the Weimar Republic was established was the outbreak of the German Revolution and naval mutinies in November 1918. Refusing suicidal orders to engage the British fleet, sailors mutinied at Kiel and Wilhelmshaven, establishing workers' and soldiers' councils that spread rapidly across Germany. Fearing a violent communist revolution like the Bolshevik takeover in Russia, Chancellor Max von Baden announced the Kaiser's abdication on 9 November, and SPD leader Friedrich Ebert formed a provisional republic to restore democratic order.

Furthermore, establishment was driven by Germany’s catastrophic military defeat in the First World War. Following the failure of the 1918 Spring Offensive and the breakthrough of Allied forces on the Western Front, the Supreme Army Command under Field Marshal Hindenburg and General Ludendorff recognized that Germany could not win. They advised the government to establish a democratic parliamentary system to secure more favorable armistice terms from US President Woodrow Wilson.

Finally, the Allied powers, particularly US President Woodrow Wilson, made the removal of autocratic militarism and the Kaiser a mandatory condition for peace. To stop the starvation caused by the Allied naval blockade and prevent a total Allied military invasion of Germany, democratic politicians in the Reichstag drafted a progressive democratic constitution at Weimar in 1919.

sources.title: Source D: Reich President Friedrich Ebert's Address to the Weimar National Assembly (6 February 1919)
sources.text: The German people are now their own masters. Imperialism and militarism have collapsed; arbitrary rule is ended forever. We must replace violence with law, and dictatorship with constitutional freedom. Our task is to establish a republic rooted in social democracy and public justice. But we warn our adversaries abroad: do not drive the German people to utter desperation. A democratic Germany cannot bear a peace of vengeance that enslaves our working people or dismembers our national soil.

lessons.prologue: In late October 1918, imperial Germany stood on the precipice of total exhaustion. Frontline soldiers starved on turnip soup while Allied armies breached the Hindenburg Line. When naval admirals ordered a suicidal final sortie into the North Sea, sailors at Kiel raised red flags, sparking a nationwide revolution. Within days, five centuries of monarchical rule vanished as Kaiser Wilhelm II fled across the Dutch border in the dead of night. Amidst the chaos of strikes and revolutionary councils, moderate Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert was thrust into power—proclaiming a fragile republic that was born in defeat, surrounded by enemies, and doomed to sign an armistice the army refused to acknowledge. Were the democratic foundations of the new Weimar Constitution fatally flawed from the very moment of its creation?
lessons.specification_anchor: The Weimar Republic 1918–29: the origins of the Republic, 1918–19; political unrest, the abdication of the Kaiser, armistice and the strengths and weaknesses of the Weimar Constitution.

lessons.title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
lessons.enquiry: Surrounded by enemies: How did the Weimar Republic survive the traumatic birth of the Treaty of Versailles, violent uprisings from the extreme left and right, and the catastrophic economic collapse of 1923?

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry evaluates the existential political and economic challenges that threatened the Weimar Republic between 1919 and 1923, investigating the territorial, military, and financial terms of the Treaty of Versailles, the Dolchstoßlegende myth, the left-wing Spartacist Uprising, the right-wing Kapp Putsch, right-wing political assassinations, and the 1923 French occupation of the Ruhr that triggered runaway hyperinflation.

objectives.objective: Explain how the Treaty of Versailles and the "stab-in-the-back" myth alienated German nationalists from the Republic.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2] and Source A (Versailles political cartoon). Highlight territorial losses (Alsace-Lorraine, Polish Corridor), the 100,000 army cap, Article 231 War Guilt, and £6.6bn reparations branded as the "Diktat".
objectives.question: How did the terms of the Treaty of Versailles foster deep nationalist hatred toward the "November Criminals" who founded the Weimar Republic?

objectives.objective: Analyse the Spartacist Uprising of January 1919 and the consequences of Ebert’s reliance on the Freikorps.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2]. Emphasize that Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht’s communist revolt was violently crushed by right-wing Freikorps mercenaries, creating permanent socialist-communist division.
objectives.question: Why did the brutal suppression of the Spartacist Uprising create a lasting divide on the German political left?

objectives.objective: Evaluate the Kapp Putsch of March 1920 and explain why General von Seeckt’s army refused to defend the government.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [3.1]–[3.2] and Source B (Freikorps occupying Berlin). Contrast General von Seeckt’s refusal ("Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr") with the general strike of trade unionists that defeated the putsch.
objectives.question: Why did the Kapp Putsch reveal the dangerous disloyalty of the regular German army toward the democratic Republic?

objectives.objective: Examine the wave of right-wing political assassinations and the profound judicial bias in Weimar courts.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [4.1]–[4.2]. Focus on Organization Consul murdering Matthias Erzberger and Walter Rathenau, and how conservative judges granted lenient sentences to nationalist killers while punishing left-wing rebels harshly.
objectives.question: How did judicial bias in Weimar courtrooms protect right-wing nationalist assassins while undermining public faith in democracy?

objectives.objective: Assess how the French occupation of the Ruhr and the policy of passive resistance triggered catastrophic hyperinflation in 1923.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [5.1]–[5.2] and Source C (50 Million Mark Banknote). Explain that French troops seized industrial assets, passive resistance halted production, and the government printed unbacked money, wiping out middle-class savings.
objectives.question: Why did the German government’s response to the French invasion of the Ruhr result in runaway hyperinflation?

video.title: Jan 1919: The 'Spartacist' Revolt | GCSE History Revision | Weimar & Nazi Germany
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–03:15 | Lesson Phase: Left-Wing Threat | Tone Alert: Focuses on the January 1919 Berlin uprising led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, and Ebert's reliance on the Freikorps.
video.viewing_task:
[00:55] Recall: Who were the leaders of the Spartacist League, and what type of government did they seek to establish?
[02:15] Cause & Consequence: Why did President Ebert turn to the right-wing Freikorps to crush the Spartacists, and what dangerous precedent did this set?
video.model_answer: The Spartacists were led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, seeking a communist council republic modelled on Soviet Russia. Ebert made a pact with the army and nationalist Freikorps paramilitaries because the regular army was demoralised; this set a fatal precedent of relying on violent anti-democratic soldiers to defend a democratic state.

video.title: 1920: The Kapp Putsch (& Ongoing Political Violence) | GCSE History Revision
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–04:00 | Lesson Phase: Right-Wing Threat | Tone Alert: Examines Wolfgang Kapp and General Lüttwitz's march on Berlin, the army's refusal to fire ('Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr'), and the general strike.
video.viewing_task:
[01:20] Key Question: When the Weimar government ordered the army to defend Berlin against the Kapp Putsch, how did General von Seeckt respond?
[02:50] Evaluation: How was the Kapp Putsch ultimately defeated, and what did it reveal about the loyalty of the German civil service and army?
video.model_answer: General von Seeckt famously declared 'Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr', refusing to deploy troops against right-wing former soldiers. The putsch was defeated by a nationwide general strike called by Berlin trade unions and workers that cut transport, water, and power, proving the army could not be relied upon to defend democracy.

video.title: 1923: Hyperinflation | GCSE History | Weimar Germany

video.viewing_task:
[01:10] Cause: Why did French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr in January 1923?
[02:30] Consequence: Which social class suffered the most devastating economic loss during the 1923 hyperinflation, and why?
video.model_answer: France and Belgium invaded the industrial Ruhr because Germany failed to deliver promised timber and coal reparations installments. The German middle class (Mittelstand) suffered worst because lifelong savings, war bonds, and fixed pension incomes became completely worthless overnight, while debts and mortgages held by big industrialists were wiped out.

learning_objectives.overarching: To understand the severe threats to the Weimar Republic from 1919 to 1923.
scaffolded: Demonstrate precise knowledge of the terms of the Treaty of Versailles and explain why many Germans saw it as a 'diktat' and a national humiliation.
Analyse the differing threats posed by left-wing uprisings (the Spartacist revolt, 1919) and right-wing challenges (the Kapp Putsch, 1920), evaluating why the government survived both.
Evaluate the causes and devastating impact of the 1923 hyperinflation crisis, using specific evidence to show how it destroyed the savings and trust of the German middle class.

narrative_blocks.title: Red Flags in Berlin: The Spartacist Uprising and the Freikorps Bloodbath (Jan 1919)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.1] In January 1919, radical left-wing revolutionaries mounted a violent armed assault against the new republican government. Led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, the **Spartacist Communist uprising** mobilized over one hundred thousand armed workers in Berlin, seizing railway junctions, newspaper offices, and government buildings in an attempt to overthrow Ebert and establish a Soviet-style workers' council dictatorship. [1.2] Lacking reliable police, Defense Minister Gustav Noske authorized aggressive **Freikorps paramilitary deployment**, unleashing demobilized imperial soldiers armed with machine guns and flamethrowers to crush the revolt in the streets. Over one hundred workers were killed in fierce urban combat, culminating when **Rosa Luxemburg murdered** alongside Liebknecht by right-wing soldiers, creating a permanent, bitter rift between Social Democrats and Communists.

sources.model_answer: Source A reveals that left-wing revolutionaries possessed heavy military equipment, field artillery, and machine guns, occupying vital national monuments and government buildings across Berlin. narrative_blocks.title: The Diktat of Versailles: War Guilt, Reparations and the 'Stab in the Back' Legend (Jun 1919)
narrative_blocks.text: [2.1] On 28 June 1919, German delegates were forced to sign the Treaty of Versailles under threat of immediate Allied invasion. Denounced across the political spectrum as a humiliating diktat, the treaty enforced the punitive **Article 231 War Guilt** clause, requiring Germany to accept sole moral responsibility for the war and justifying astronomical **£6.6 billion reparations** payments to Allied powers. [2.2] Germany lost thirteen percent of its European territory, its overseas colonies, and had its army capped at one hundred thousand volunteers. Nationalist circles bitterly blamed democratic politicians for accepting these catastrophic terms, aggressively promoting the **'Dolchstoss' backstab myth**, which falsely alleged that the German army was undefeated on the battlefield but betrayed from within by socialists and Jews.

narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 2: How did the Versailles Treaty foster deep nationalist hatred of the Republic?
paragraphs: [2.1] On 28 June 1919, German delegates were forced to sign the Treaty of Versailles under threat of immediate Allied invasion. Denounced across the political spectrum as a humiliating diktat, the treaty enforced the punitive **Article 231 War Guilt** clause, requiring Germany to accept sole moral responsibility for the war and justifying astronomical **£6.6 billion reparations** payments to Allied powers.

[2.2] Germany lost thirteen percent of its European territory, its overseas colonies, and had its army capped at one hundred thousand volunteers. Nationalist circles bitterly blamed democratic politicians for accepting these catastrophic terms, aggressively promoting the **'Dolchstoss' backstab myth**, which falsely alleged that the German army was undefeated on the battlefield but betrayed from within by socialists and Jews.

narrative_blocks.title: The Ehrhardt Brigade Marches: The Kapp Putsch and the General Strike (Mar 1920)
narrative_blocks.text: [3.1] In March 1920, the government faced a dangerous insurrection from the extreme right when it attempted to disband the Freikorps under Versailles treaty obligations. Nationalists launched the **Wolfgang Kapp putsch**, marching five thousand armed troops into Berlin and seizing government ministries, forcing Ebert and his cabinet to flee the capital for Stuttgart to avoid arrest. [3.2] When Ebert ordered the regular army to intervene, he encountered **General von Seeckt refusal**, who coldly proclaimed that "Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr". The republic was rescued not by the military, but by a massive nationwide **Berlin general strike** called by trade unions, which paralyzed gas, water, and transport services, causing the putsch to collapse within four days.

sources.caption: Mutinous soldiers of the Ehrhardt Naval Brigade wearing swastika-painted steel helmets occupying the government district in Berlin during the right-wing Kapp Putsch.

sources.context: Freikorps troops of Marinebrigade Ehrhardt occupying Berlin during the Kapp Putsch in March 1920.
sources.enquiry_question: How useful is Source C for an enquiry into the military weaknesses of the Weimar government between 1919 and 1923?
sources.model_answer:
Content & Contextual Knowledge: Source C is exceptionally useful because it provides undeniable physical evidence that the Weimar Republic was fundamentally vulnerable to right-wing paramilitary rebellion. The photograph shows heavily armed troops of Marinebrigade Ehrhardt wearing swastika-painted steel helmets and occupying the central government district in Berlin. This reflects precise historical events: in March 1920, when Chancellor Bauer's government attempted to disband the 5,000-strong Ehrhardt brigade to comply with Versailles treaty troop caps of 100,000 men, the Freikorps marched into Berlin and proclaimed Wolfgang Kapp as Chancellor. When the government ordered army chief General Hans von Seeckt to suppress the rebellion, Seeckt famously refused, stating that "Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr", forcing Ebert's elected cabinet to flee the capital to Dresden and Stuttgart.

Provenance & Utility Evaluation: As an authentic press photograph captured on the Wilhelmstraße during the coup (nature and origin), the source captures the brazen defiance and military power of demobilised veteran paramilitaries who despised the democratic republic. However, the photograph only shows the initial armed takeover; it does not show why the putsch ultimately failed within four days, namely that Berlin's trade unions launched a massive general strike that cut off water, gas, electricity, and rail transport, paralyzing the coup leaders and demonstrating that working-class solidarity—rather than the state's military—saved the Weimar democracy in 1920.

narrative_blocks.title: Bullets from the Shadows: The Assassinations of Erzberger and Rathenau (1921–1922)
narrative_blocks.text: [4.1] Defeated in open coup attempts, right-wing extremists turned to covert political murder, orchestrating systematic **Organisation Consul terror** campaigns against prominent republican leaders. In August 1921, armistice signatory **Matthias Erzberger assassinated** by nationalist hit-squads while walking in the Black Forest, demonized as a traitor for signing the surrender and implementing democratic tax reforms that burdened wealthy elites. [4.2] In June 1922, foreign minister **Walther Rathenau murdered** by machine-gun fire and hand grenades hurled into his open car in Berlin. As a wealthy Jewish industrialist who pursued reconciliation with Western powers, Rathenau was despised by anti-Semitic nationalists. Over 350 political assassinations occurred between 1919 and 1922, with right-wing judges handing down notoriously lenient sentences to nationalist killers.

narrative_blocks.title: French Troops in the Ruhr & The Mark Collapses: The Nightmare of Hyperinflation (1923)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.1] In January 1923, after Germany defaulted on timber and coal deliveries, sixty thousand French and Belgian troops carried out the **Ruhr industrial occupation** to seize reparations by force. Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno ordered a policy of **passive strike resistance**, instructing coal miners and railway workers to refuse cooperation while the German government paid their lost wages by printing billions of paper marks. [5.2] This reckless money printing triggered a catastrophic **hyperinflation currency collapse**, rendering the German mark worthless by autumn 1923. Citizens carried wheelbarrows of cash to purchase basic loaves of bread, while middle-class bank savings, pensions, and insurance policies were completely wiped out. Although debts were eliminated, hyperinflation shattered middle-class faith in the democratic Weimar Republic.

sources.enquiry_question: What does Source E reveal about the severity of the economic collapse confronting Germany in the autumn of 1923?
sources.model_answer: Source E provides direct material proof of the total hyperinflationary collapse of the German currency. Printed in denominations of 1,000,000,000,000 (one trillion) marks, the banknote was printed only on one side with coarse paper because the Reichsbank’s printing presses could not keep pace with spiraling inflation and running out of ink. Historically, the crisis was triggered when 60,000 French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr industrial basin in January 1923 after Germany defaulted on reparations; the Weimar government ordered passive resistance and printed trillions of unbacked paper marks to pay striking miners. By November 1923, an egg cost 320 billion marks, paper money had lost all functional value, and workers were forced to collect wages twice daily in laundry baskets and wheelbarrows before prices doubled by nightfall.

questions.question: Explain why there were challenges to the Weimar Republic from both the left and right in the years 1919–1923. [12 marks]
questions.model:
One decisive reason for challenges to Weimar was right-wing nationalist fury over the Treaty of Versailles and the 'stab-in-the-back' myth (Dolchstoßlegende). Nationalists, military elites, and Freikorps paramilitaries viewed the war guilt clause (Article 231) and £6.6 billion reparations as national humiliations, branding democratic politicians 'November Criminals'. Therefore, this caused right-wing challenges because right-wing militarists refused to accept military defeat, launching putsches like the 1920 Kapp Putsch to overthrow the democratic system they despised.

Furthermore, challenges erupted from radical left-wing communists inspired by the 1917 Russian Bolshevik Revolution. The Spartacist League (KPD), led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, rejected parliamentary democracy, demanding that power belong to workers' councils. In January 1919, 100,000 workers staged armed uprisings in Berlin, seizing railway stations and newspaper offices. Therefore, this caused left-wing challenges because radical communists actively attempted to overthrow Ebert’s moderate regime through armed urban revolution.

Finally, challenges escalated due to the catastrophic economic ruin triggered by the 1923 French occupation of the Ruhr and hyperinflation. When French troops occupied the industrial Ruhr after Germany defaulted on timber and coal payments, the government ordered passive resistance and printed vast amounts of unbacked paper marks. This caused hyperinflation, wiping out the life savings of the middle class. Therefore, this provoked severe challenges because economic devastation destroyed public confidence in democracy, encouraging uprisings like Hitler's Munich Putsch in November 1923.

Taken on the streets of Berlin by a contemporary press photographer, its candid origin documents both monarchist defiance and the republic's military vulnerability, though a single street scene cannot show the Berlin workers' general strike that defeated Kapp after four days.

Source C is equally useful because it illuminates the devastating economic crisis that destabilised Weimar society in 1923. The autumn 1923 Berlin photograph depicts three young children stacking dozens of tightly bound bundles of Reichsbank banknotes into a courtyard pyramid because paper money was worth less than wooden blocks. Contextual knowledge confirms that after Germany missed reparations deliveries under the £6.6 billion settlement and Franco-Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr in January 1923, the government printed money to fund "passive resistance", driving a loaf of bread to 200 billion marks by November 1923 and wiping out Mittelstand savings and pensions. Although posed for dramatic effect to shock newspaper readers with the absurdity of currency collapse, that visual immediacy makes Source C invaluable evidence of how hyperinflation eroded middle-class faith in Weimar democracy.

questions.question: Question 3(b): Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the challenges facing the Weimar Republic in the years 1919–1923. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations. [4 marks]

interpretations.title: Interpretation 1: Political Violence and Military Disloyalty
interpretations.provenance: From The Coming of the Third Reich by Richard J. Evans, published in 2003.
interpretations.content: The gravest challenges confronting the early Weimar Republic were political violence, extremist insurrections, and the open disloyalty of the army. From the outset, the republic was assaulted by armed uprisings from both the extreme left and the extreme right. The Kapp Putsch of March 1920 demonstrated that the regular military could not be relied upon to defend the constitution, while nationalist assassination squads murdered over three hundred political figures, including Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau. It was this violent lawlessness that brought the republic to the verge of collapse.

interpretations.title: Interpretation 2: Economic Catastrophe and Hyperinflation
interpretations.provenance: From A History of Germany 1918–2014 by Mary Fulbrook, published in 2014.
interpretations.content: The Weimar Republic was shaken far more profoundly by economic catastrophe than by right-wing putsches. The crippling burden of reparations, exacerbated by the French occupation of the Ruhr in January 1923, triggered hyperinflation that completely destroyed the German currency. The economic collapse wiped out the life savings, pensions, and financial security of the respectable middle class. This alienated millions of ordinary citizens from the democratic system, leaving a permanent legacy of bitterness and cynicism towards the republic.

questions.examiner_tip: Contrast the core threat identified by each historian: Evans (Interpretation 1) argues armed political violence and army disloyalty were the gravest danger, whereas Fulbrook (Interpretation 2) argues economic collapse and hyperinflation damaged the republic far more deeply.

scaffolding.acronym: AO4 Evaluative Verdict: Weigh Both Views + Own Knowledge + Criteria (25 mins)
scaffolding.guidance: Construct a balanced evaluation of Interpretation 2 against Interpretation 1 on the challenges facing the Weimar Republic in the years 1919–1923, integrating contextual knowledge, analysing how the authors convey their views, and reaching a criteria-led verdict.
sentence_starters: Interpretation 2 presents a persuasive case that...
This view is strongly supported by contextual knowledge, as...
However, Interpretation 1 challenges this emphasis by arguing that...
Noticeably, the two historians convey contrasting tones: Interpretation 2 uses language such as "...", whereas Interpretation 1 stresses "..."
Overall, judged by the criterion of..., I agree with Interpretation 2 to a [large / partial / limited] extent because...
checklist: Evaluated Interpretation 2 using verbatim quotations and precise own contextual knowledge.
Evaluated Interpretation 1 as a counter-perspective using verbatim quotations and independent own knowledge.
Analysed how the authors' language, tone, or selection of evidence conveys their differing views.
Reached a sustained, criteria-led overall judgement with accurate specialist terminology (4/4 SPaG).

questions.model:
Interpretation 2 advances a highly convincing argument that economic catastrophe inflicted deeper, longer-lasting damage on the Weimar Republic than armed insurrections. Mary Fulbrook contends that Weimar "was shaken far more profoundly by economic catastrophe than by right-wing putsches", pointing to reparations, the January 1923 Ruhr occupation, and hyperinflation that "completely destroyed the German currency." Contextual knowledge strongly corroborates this: saddled with £6.6 billion in reparations in May 1921, Germany defaulted on coal and timber deliveries, prompting 60,000 French and Belgian troops to occupy the industrial Ruhr. Chancellor Cuno's policy of printing unbacked paper Marks to pay striking workers during "passive resistance" pushed the exchange rate to 4.2 trillion Marks to the dollar by November 1923. As Fulbrook highlights, this "wiped out the life savings, pensions, and financial security of the respectable middle class." Unlike street rebellions that collapsed within days, hyperinflation penalised thrifty Mittelstand savers, artisans, and pensioners across every German town, breeding "a permanent legacy of bitterness and cynicism" that later made middle-class voters receptive to nationalist extremism.

Nevertheless, Interpretation 1 provides an essential counter-perspective by demonstrating that without surviving repeated armed rebellions, the republic would have fallen long before 1923. Richard J. Evans argues that the "gravest challenges" were "political violence, extremist insurrections, and the open disloyalty of the army." This is substantiated by relentless left- and right-wing bloodshed: the communist Spartacist Uprising of January 1919, the Red Ruhr Army revolt of 1920, and Hitler's Munich Putsch in November 1923. Crucially, Evans stresses that the March 1920 Kapp Putsch proved "the regular military could not be relied upon to defend the constitution" when General von Seeckt refused to fire on Marinebrigade Ehrhardt, leaving only a trade-union general strike to rescue Ebert's government. Furthermore, right-wing Organisation Consul gunmen carried out 376 political assassinations—including Matthias Erzberger (1921) and Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau (June 1922)—while conservative judges handed right-wing killers lenient sentences, exposing deep institutional rot.

Noticeably, the historians convey contrasting judgements through comparative and emphatic language: Fulbrook explicitly ranks threats ("shaken far more profoundly... than by right-wing putsches") to emphasise mass psychological alienation, whereas Evans uses urgent crisis imagery ("assaulted", "violent lawlessness", "verge of collapse") to foreground immediate physical overthrow. Overall, judged by breadth and permanence of impact, I largely agree with Interpretation 2: while paramilitary violence and judicial-military disloyalty posed acute existential emergencies between 1919 and 1922, every putsch failed, whereas the 1923 hyperinflation trauma permanently severed millions of ordinary middle-class citizens from loyalty to Weimar democracy.

tier_4m.title: 4/16 Basic Description
tier_4m.text: I agree with Interpretation 2 because it says hyperinflation destroyed the German currency in 1923 after France invaded the Ruhr, and middle-class people lost all their savings. However, Interpretation 1 says political violence was worse because of the Kapp Putsch in 1920 and over three hundred political murders.
tier_4m.verdict: AO4 Level 1 (4 marks) • SPaG Threshold (1 mark). Paraphrases surface claims from both interpretations with minimal independent detail and no analytical weighing.

tier_8m.text:

After Germany missed £6.6 billion reparations payments, France occupied the Ruhr in January 1923. Printing money for passive resistance caused hyperinflation where bread cost 200 billion marks, wiping out middle-class savings and turning respectable citizens against democracy.

On the other hand, Interpretation 1 argues that "political violence, extremist insurrections, and the open disloyalty of the army" were the gravest threats. Ebert faced the Spartacists in 1919, the Kapp Putsch in March 1920 when von Seeckt refused to fire on the Freikorps, and 376 assassinations including Walther Rathenau. Overall, I agree more with Interpretation 2 because hyperinflation affected the whole population rather than just Berlin or Munich.
tier_8m.verdict: AO4 Level 2/3 (8 marks) • SPaG Intermediate (2 marks). Supports both interpretations with accurate contextual facts and states a conclusion, but does not analyse how the authors convey their views or develop sustained weighing criteria.

interpretations.title: Interpretation 1: Political Violence and Military Disloyalty
interpretations.provenance: From The Coming of the Third Reich by Richard J. Evans, published in 2003.
interpretations.content: The gravest challenges confronting the early Weimar Republic were political violence, extremist insurrections, and the open disloyalty of the army. From the outset, the republic was assaulted by armed uprisings from both the extreme left and the extreme right. The Kapp Putsch of March 1920 demonstrated that the regular military could not be relied upon to defend the constitution, while nationalist assassination squads murdered over three hundred political figures, including Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau. It was this violent lawlessness that brought the republic to the verge of collapse.

interpretations.title: Interpretation 2: Economic Catastrophe and Hyperinflation
interpretations.provenance: From A History of Germany 1918–2014 by Mary Fulbrook, published in 2014.
interpretations.content: The Weimar Republic was shaken far more profoundly by economic catastrophe than by right-wing putsches. The crippling burden of reparations, exacerbated by the French occupation of the Ruhr in January 1923, triggered hyperinflation that completely destroyed the German currency. The economic collapse wiped out the life savings, pensions, and financial security of the respectable middle class. This alienated millions of ordinary citizens from the democratic system, leaving a permanent legacy of bitterness and cynicism towards the republic.

tasks.text: Explain why there were challenges to the Weimar Republic from both the left and right in the years 1919–1923. [12 marks]
tasks.model:
One major reason the Weimar Republic faced severe challenges was the outrage caused by the Treaty of Versailles (1919). Signed in June 1919, the treaty imposed the devastating Article 231 War Guilt clause, £6.6 billion in reparations, lost 13% of German European territory, and drastically reduced the army to 100,000 men. German nationalists condemned the Weimar politicians as the 'November Criminals' who had 'stabbed Germany in the back' (the Dolchstoss myth). This fueled right-wing paramilitary putsches, such as the 1920 Kapp Putsch, where Wolfgang Kapp and the Freikorps seized Berlin while the army refused to defend the republic.

Furthermore, the Republic was threatened by violent uprisings from the extreme left, notably the Spartacist Uprising of January 1919. Led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, communist revolutionaries seized newspaper offices and attempted to establish a Soviet-style communist state. President Ebert was forced to rely on right-wing Freikorps paramilitaries to violently crush the workers, permanently fracturing the German working class and leaving left-wing parties bitter enemies of the moderate SPD.

Finally, challenges culminated in the 1923 French occupation of the Ruhr and runaway hyperinflation. When Germany missed timber and coal reparations, 60,000 French and Belgian troops occupied the industrial heartland of the Ruhr. The government called for passive resistance and printed trillions of paper marks to pay striking workers, causing catastrophic hyperinflation that destroyed the savings of the middle class and severely undermined faith in democratic institutions.

lessons.prologue: Between 1919 and 1923, the young Weimar Republic fought for its survival against assassins, putschists, and economic catastrophe. The signing of the Treaty of Versailles stunned the German public, cementing the toxic 'Stab in the Back' myth that democratic politicians had betrayed an undefeated army. On the streets of Berlin, Communist Spartacists battled right-wing Freikorps mercenaries in bloody barricade warfare. When French and Belgian troops seized the Ruhr in January 1923, the government's desperate policy of passive resistance triggered catastrophic hyperinflation—wiping out the life savings of the middle class and leaving millions carrying laundry baskets of worthless cash to buy a single loaf of bread. How did the young republic manage to survive the combined onslaught of political assassinations, extremist putsches, and catastrophic hyperinflation?

lessons.title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
lessons.enquiry: Dancing on a volcano: Did Gustav Stresemann genuinely rescue the Weimar Republic from the ashes of 1923, or was Germany's 'Golden Age' built on quicksand?

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry evaluates the apparent stabilization of the Weimar Republic during the "Golden Twenties" under Gustav Stresemann, examining the Rentenmark currency reform, the Dawes Plan of 1924, American Wall Street loans, the Locarno Treaties of 1925, Germany’s admission to the League of Nations in 1926, the Kellogg-Briand Pact, the Young Plan of 1929, and Stresemann’s prophetic warning that Germany was "dancing on a volcano".

objectives.objective: Explain how Gustav Stresemann halted passive resistance and stabilized the currency with the Rentenmark in late 1923.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2]. Emphasize that Stresemann ended the ruinous Ruhr strike and introduced the Rentenmark, strictly backed by agricultural and industrial land mortgages to stop hyperinflation.
objectives.question: How did the introduction of the Rentenmark restore public confidence in the German monetary system in late 1923?

objectives.objective: Analyse the mechanisms of the Dawes Plan (1924) and the impact of American loans on German industrial recovery.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2]. Highlight that the Dawes Plan rescheduled reparations, secured French withdrawal from the Ruhr, and injected 800 million gold marks in US loans to modernize industry.
objectives.question: Why did American loans under the Dawes Plan create a rapid economic boom while leaving Germany financially vulnerable?

objectives.objective: Evaluate the diplomatic significance of the 1925 Locarno Treaties in breaking Germany’s post-war international isolation.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [3.1]–[3.2]. Detail Stresemann’s policy of fulfillment, the voluntary guarantee of western frontiers with France and Belgium, and the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Stresemann and Briand.
objectives.question: How did the Locarno Treaties transform Germany’s diplomatic relationship with Britain and France?

objectives.objective: Assess the political impact of Germany’s entry into the League of Nations with a permanent Council seat in 1926.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [4.1]–[4.2]. Focus on Germany’s rehabilitation as a recognized great power, Stresemann’s speech in Geneva, and the restoration of national pride.
objectives.question: Why was admission to the League of Nations with a permanent Council seat a major foreign policy triumph for Gustav Stresemann?

objectives.objective: Assess the Young Plan of 1929 and explain why Stresemann warned that Germany was "dancing on a volcano".
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [5.1]–[5.2]. Contrast the reduction of reparations to £2bn with right-wing opposition led by Hugenberg and Hitler, and explain how dependency on short-term US loans proved fatal in October 1929.
objectives.question: Why did Gustav Stresemann describe Germany’s economic recovery as "dancing on a volcano" shortly before the Wall Street Crash?

source_context.Source A: At the October 1925 Locarno Conference, Stresemann signed treaties accepting Germany's western borders with France and Belgium, earning Germany European respectability and paving the way for Allied troop withdrawal from the Rhineland. Hinge Question: Why did Stresemann agree to guarantee Germany's western borders with France and Belgium while refusing to give similar guarantees for its eastern borders with Poland and Czechoslovakia?
source_context.Source B: The Dawes Plan of 1924 reorganised German reparations payments and provided an initial loan of 800 million gold marks funded heavily by Wall Street bankers, triggering an unprecedented industrial boom. Hinge Question: How did the Dawes Plan create a dangerous economic cycle where Germany relied entirely on American loans to pay British and French reparations?
source_context.Source C: Signed in Paris in 1928 by 62 nations, the Kellogg-Briand Pact outlawed aggressive war, demonstrating Germany's reintegration as a trusted great power, though nationalists attacked it for renouncing the military reconquest of lost territories. Hinge Question: Why did German nationalist parties fiercely denounce Stresemann for signing the Kellogg-Briand Pact when it offered moral protection against foreign invasion?
source_context.Source D: In 1929, the Young Plan reduced total German reparations from £6.6 billion to £2 billion payable over 59 years, but media baron Alfred Hugenberg and Adolf Hitler launched a vicious campaign branding it the "enslavement of future generations". Hinge Question: How did the national campaign against the Young Plan in 1929 allow Adolf Hitler to gain nationwide mainstream political respectability and media coverage?
source_context.Source E: In September 1925, Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann was preparing to negotiate the Locarno Treaties with Britain and France, pursuing his policy of "fulfillment" while reassuring conservative monarchists that he had not abandoned German nationalist ambitions. Hinge Question: Does Source C prove that Stresemann was a cynical nationalist pretending to be a European peacemaker, or a realistic statesman protecting Germany's vital national interests?

learning_objectives.overarching: To understand Stresemann's role in stabilising the Weimar Republic during the 'Golden Age' of 1924–1929.
scaffolded: Demonstrate precise knowledge of Stresemann's economic reforms: the Rentenmark, the Dawes Plan (1924), and the Young Plan (1929).
Analyse how Stresemann's foreign policy achievements—particularly the Locarno Pact (1925) and Germany's entry into the League of Nations (1926)—restored Germany's international status.
Evaluate the extent to which the 'Golden Age' was a genuine recovery or a fragile illusion built on American loans that could collapse at any moment.

items.answer: The set of rules for how Germany would be governed as a democratic republic.

items.question: What was Proportional Representation (PR)?
items.answer: An electoral system where the percentage of votes equals the percentage of seats in the Reichstag.

items.question: Why was Proportional Representation a weakness?
items.answer: It led to dozens of tiny parties and weak coalition governments.

items.question: What was Article 48?
items.answer: It allowed the President to make laws without the Reichstag in an emergency.

items.question: Who was the first President of the Weimar Republic?
items.answer: Friedrich Ebert.

items.question: What was the 'stab in the back' myth?
items.answer: The belief that Germany was betrayed by politicians, not defeated in battle.

items.question: Who were the 'November Criminals'?
items.answer: The politicians who signed the Armistice.

items.question: When did WW1 end?
What is an 'armistice'?
items.answer: An agreement to stop fighting.

items.question: What does 'inflation' mean?
items.answer: Prices rising rapidly.

narrative_blocks.title: Burning the Trillion-Mark Notes: Stresemann and the Miracle of the Rentenmark (Nov 1923)
narrative_blocks.text: [1.1] In August 1923, at the catastrophic height of the national inflation crisis, moderate statesman **Gustav Stresemann chancellor** formed a broad "Great Coalition" government. Stresemann acted with decisive political courage, calling off passive resistance in the occupied Ruhr to halt ruinous state compensation spending and balancing the national budget by slashing bloated civil service payrolls and cutting government expenditure across all ministries. [1.2] In November 1923, Stresemann introduced the revolutionary **Rentenmark land-backed currency**, a strictly limited temporary currency mortgaged on Germany's collective industrial and agricultural land assets. The German public accepted the new notes with confidence, and when the permanent Reichsbank **Mark stabilized (1924)** under the new Reichsmark, hyperinflation was conquered, establishing the monetary bedrock for a dramatic five-year economic recovery.

sources.enquiry_question: How useful is Source A for an enquiry into how Stresemann and Schacht successfully stabilized German currency during the hyperinflation crisis of late 1923?
sources.model_answer: Source A is highly useful because it outlines the precise economic mechanism Stresemann and Schacht used to halt hyperinflation: ending the printing presses and securing the Rentenmark against physical land and industrial assets at a fixed 1:1,000,000,000,000 ratio. As an official statutory decree, it reflects government policy, though it naturally emphasizes administrative resolve over the lingering impoverishment of the middle class who lost their life savings.
